content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper claims to propose a unified method for weighting examples while training. It first gives some survey on recent baseline methods and argue that there are disagreements on which samples, easy or hard, to learn first. Their method, dubbed as FlexW, is shown to contain some baselines methods, like Focal loss or SPL, and by tuning some hyperparameters, FlexW is shown to achieve slightly better performance than others.
content.main_review:
Strength:

1. The paper gives an extensive survey on the existing weighting scheme (Figure 1) and propose a general one (Eq.(11)) that can contain others. 
2. Depending on different hyperparameters used, FlexW is shown to achieve better results than the baselines. 

Weakness:

1. It is not clear how to choose the hyperparameters of (11) and determine which weighting schemes, i.e., among easy-first, medium-first, hard-first, to use for given data. The paper does not describe the details on this process, which significantly undermines the practicality of their method. With this reason alone, I do not think the work is enough for a publication at ICLR.

We thank the reviewer for providing valuable feedback to our manuscript. We hope that our response can solve your concerns ("Weakness" section). 

**Concern: It is not clear how to choose the hyperparameters of (11) and determine which weighting schemes, i.e., among easy-first, medium-first, hard-first, to use for given data. The paper does not describe the details on this process, which significantly undermines the practicality of their method.**

We apologize for missing the detailed analysis of how the weighting function can implement these three priority modes. In the new manuscript, we added the following content:

First, in Section B.5 of the new manuscript, we explained how the weight function implements these three priority modes. The priority modes that the weight function can achieve are determined by the attributes of the function. Second, we added the parameter value intervals in which the performance is stable in the new manuscript (Section B.7). What's more, in Section 5.7, we also gave the recommended parameter values for the three priority modes. 

Just like other hyper-parameters in the training process such as learning rate, the hyper-parameters in the weighting function can also be obtained through grid search within the given parameter value intervals. Our experiments have verified that the effect is stable when parameters are selected within these ranges. display_title: Official Review of Paper801 by Reviewer 3h4h

content.summary_of_the_paper: In the paper, the authors try to answer the question of whether easy or hard data should be learned first for a task in the sample weighting approach. They propose a high-level unified weighted loss to explore this question theoretically and a flexible weighting scheme to overcome the defects of existing weighting schemes. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified through experiments on image classification, graph classification and object detection.
content.main_review:
Strength:
1. Figure 1 in the paper shows a comprehensive summary of existing weighting schemes in different domains, which is helpful for readers to get an overview of existing sample weighting-based methods. 
2. Experiments on various settings show the proposed method is better than the baselines.

Weakness:
1. The core concepts of the paper, easy or hard samples, are not well defined. It's better to have a definition of the meaning of easy/medium/hard because the words are quite relative (via comparisons). Does it depend on to what extent the data can be correctly classified?
2. Prior knowledge of "hard"-first or "easy"-first is still needed through a way of assigning values to two hyperparameters of the proposed method. It is unknown that how these hyperparameters are chosen. Also, if such prior knowledge is known, some other corresponding weighting methods can be applied accordingly. 

Comments:
1. The authors claim that "an ideal weighting strategy should let the weights for noisy samples to be reduced". How does the proposed method distinguish whether a "hard" sample is a noisy sample (should downweigh it) or it is a valuable sample (should upweigh it, such as in class imbalance setting)?
2. How to integrate the prior knowledge for the cases where we have both class imbalance and label noise in the data? Is it possible to handle this complex case for the proposed method?
3. I have some doubts about the results of label noise experiments, i.e., Table 1. In label noise setting, overfitting label noise/applying hard-first mode at the beginning of the training would be very harmful. How could FlexW (hard-first) largely outperforms some easy-first baselines in label noise learning, such as S-model and Co-teaching?
4. Importance sampling is a classic and important weighting method. I suggest adding it in Figure 1 and having some discussions about it.
content.summary_of_the_review: The research problem is important, but some key parts of the proposed method are not well defined/explained, such as how to choose the hyperparameters related to prior knowledge, how to define hard/easy-first. I also have some doubts about how the proposed method could achieve such a good performance on label noise experiments.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3h4h (Part 1)
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the careful reading and providing valuable feedback to our manuscript. We hope that our response can solve your concerns ("Weakness" and "Comments" sections). 

**Concern 1: The core concepts of the paper, easy or hard samples, are not well defined. It's better to have a definition of the meaning of easy/medium/hard because the words are quite relative (via comparisons). Does it depend on to what extent the data can be correctly classified?**

Thank you for pointing out the problem, we have added this content in the new manuscript (Section 3.1). Like most existing weighting schemes, such as Focal loss and SPL, this paper uses the loss as a measurement for the learning difficulty of samples which is easy to calculate and effective in various learning tasks. There are also some other criteria which are summarized in Section 3.1. 

**Concern 2: Prior knowledge of "hard"-first or "easy"-first is still needed through a way of assigning values to two hyperparameters of the proposed method. It is unknown that how these hyperparameters are chosen. Also, if such prior knowledge is known, some other corresponding weighting methods can be applied accordingly.**
1. For our method, prior knowledge is not always needed. When there is not any prior knowledge, our method can achieve these three priority modes and the best one can be selected based on the validation set.
2. We apologize for missing the detailed analysis of how the weighting function can implement the three priority modes and the detailed parameter value intervals for the three priority modes. First, in Section B.5 of the new manuscript, we added how the weight function implements these three priority modes. The priority modes that the weighting function can achieve are determined by the attributes of the function. Then, we added the parameter value intervals in which the performance is stable in the new manuscript (Section B.7). In Section 5.7, we also gave the recommended parameter values for the three priority modes. Just like other hyper-parameters in the training process such as learning rate, the hyper-parameters in the weighting function can also be obtained through grid search within the given parameter value intervals. Our experiments verified that the performance is stable when parameters are selected within these intervals.
The stable parameter intervals of $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ corresponding to different priority modes are shown in the following table:
|Priority|     Easy-first|Medium-first|     Hard-first|two-ends-first|
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
|Intervals|[0.2,0.6]×[0.9,1.2]; [-0.6,-0.2]×[0.1,0.4]|[0.2,0.6]×[0.4,0.8]|[0.2,0.6]×[0.1,0.4]; [-0.6,-0.2]×[0.9,1.2]|[-0.6,-0.2]×[0.4,0.8]|
3. Compared with existing weighting strategies, our method has the following advantages:
   1. Can not rely on prior knowledge.
   2. Implement all three priority modes.
   3. Can change priority mode during training.
   4. Obtain competitive performances in all scenarios of our experiments.

**Concern 3: The authors claim that "an ideal weighting strategy should let the weights for noisy samples to be reduced". How does the proposed method distinguish whether a "hard" sample is a noisy sample (should downweigh it) or it is a valuable sample (should upweigh it, such as in class imbalance setting)?**

Noise samples can be considered as quiet-hard samples. It is difficult to effectively distinguish hard samples from noisy samples only by relying on a single measurement because they have a common feature: large loss. Although our method cannot effectively distinguish between noisy samples and hard ones, when noise and imbalance both appear in a data set, under the priority mode of easy-first, we can adjust the category factor shown in Eq.(12) to increase the weights of samples in tail categories. Under this weighting strategy, the model can focus on the samples in tail categories without paying too much attention to the noise samples. 

**Concern 4: How to integrate the prior knowledge for the cases where we have both class imbalance and label noise in the data? Is it possible to handle this complex case for the proposed method?**
1. We discussed the occasion where both the deviations exist in Section 5.6. The results are shown in Table A-13 and Table A-14. The basic conclusion we obtained is that when both imbalance and noise exist in a data set, the strategy with a more serious deviation should be selected. 
2. In addition, to further improve the effect, the settings of the weighing scheme can refer to the response to Concern 3.
3. Another way is to directly perform a grid search in the given parameter intervals of the three priority modes, and the most suitable choice of hyper-parameters (priority mode) can be selected based on the effect of the validation set.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3h4h (Part 2)
content.comment:
**Concern 5: I have some doubts about the results of label noise experiments, i.e., Table 1. In label noise setting, overfitting label noise/applying hard-first mode at the beginning of the training would be very harmful. How could FlexW (hard-first) largely outperforms some easy-first baselines in label noise learning, such as S-model and Co-teaching?**

Relying on the value of the loss to distinguish noise is not completely accurate. However, it is a reasonable measurement because the average loss of noise samples is always higher than that of clean ones as shown in Figure A-9. Therefore, increasing the weight of samples with large losses also increases the weight of samples that are difficult but valuable, so that the classification performance of hard samples can also be improved. This is the main reason why the hard-first methods can also achieve acceptable results in some cases. We can see that the performances of the hard-first mode will not exceed that of the same method under the easy-first mode.  It also indicates that a more effective measurement is indeed important. If there is a more appropriate measurement of samples' learning difficulty $d_{i}$, $1-p_{i}$ in FlexW can be directly replaced with $d_{i}$.

**Concern 6: Importance sampling is a classic and important weighting method. I suggest adding it in Figure 1 and having some discussions about it.**

Thank you for your valuable feedback. We have added a discussion of importance sampling in the fourth paragraph of Section A in the new manuscript. Compared to the sampling-based methods, our proposed weighting scheme processes all samples every epoch, thus guaranteeing that we always know how the network is performing on each sample.

Please let us know if there are any leftover concerns and we would be happy to do our utmost to address them.

content.title: Post-rebuttal comments
content.comment:
Thank the authors very much for the rebuttal! 

After reading the rebuttal, the authors have addressed most of my concerns and I will keep my previous scoring of 5: marginally below the acceptance threshold. The proposed method integrates all three priority modes for existing weighting schemes and the best mode can be selected through evaluation on the validation set. But the authors did not provide much insight into how to choose the weighting scheme-related hyperparameters. The Table shown in the rebuttal seems quite heuristics and the results may change when the datasets/tasks are different. Besides, the proposed method uses loss as the only measurement of easy/hard samples, which may be problematic in many cases such as the co-occurrence of label noise and class imbalance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iEc4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the reading of our manuscript and providing valuable feedback. We hope that our response can solve your concerns. （To explain more clearly, we may split a concern into two pieces to answer.）

**Concern 1: All conclusions in this paper can be found from previous studies.**

To our knowledge, the following conclusions in our work are stated for the first time:

1. No one weighting scheme that can achieve all three priority modes including easy-first, medium-first, and hard-first. Our proposed weighting function can implement different priority modes, and the best one can be selected based on the validation set.

2. We obtained the conclusion that “The priority mode does not need to remain unchanged during the training process. Using varied priority modes in different training stages may achieve better results.”. The experimental results are shown in Table A-15 in the appendix.

3. For graph data set, we point out that the easy-first mode can help alleviate the over-smoothing phenomenon. The experimental results are shown in Table 5.

4. We give a clearer and comprehensive description of the relationship between the priority modes and the distribution of samples’ learning difficulty. Other weighting schemes such as Focal loss only apply one aspect of this conclusion. The experimental results are shown in Table 6.

5. We studied a situation where both noise and imbalance exist in the data set. The conclusion is that when both imbalance and noise exist, the strategy with a more serious deviation should be selected. The experimental results are shown in Table A-13 and Table A-14 in the appendix.

We will appreciate it if you find and point out references that already contain these conclusions.

**Concern 2: Although the proposed method achieved better results, it doesn't change the fact that the optimal weighting scheme still follows the same heuristics (e.g., lower weights for noisy samples, higher weights for minority samples, etc.).**

1. As stated in our paper, the optimal weighting scheme is determined by the distribution of the training samples and the prior knowledge for the task. Therefore, there is no fixed optimal weighting scheme.

2. Our method can choose the most suitable priority mode for the current data set and task based on the effect (such as accuracy) of the validation set. Thus, it is not always heuristic. After theoretical analysis and experimental verification, we got a series of conclusions shown in Section 6. When knowledge about the characteristics of the data set exists, these conclusions can be directly used to guide the choice of the optimal priority mode.

**Concern 3: The theoretical analysis conducted in the paper doesn't add much insight about how to choose the weighting scheme.**
 
Part of the theoretical analysis is indeed not a direct insight into the choice of weighting schemes. However, these analyses also has great significance of the choice of weighting schemes which can be summarized as follows:

1. To choose a suitable weighting scheme, we must first understand the intrinsic differences between different weighting schemes. The analysis of Sections 3.2 and 3.3 in the new manuscript reveals that the difference in weighting strategies lies in the different values of the thresholds $\tau$ and regularizers $R(w_{i},\Gamma,\lambda)$. Thus, there is no fixed optimal priority mode. In other words, different weighting strategies should be adopted for different situations.

2. The theoretical analysis of Section 3.4 in the new manuscript supports the second requirement in Section 3.3 which directly guides how to choose a weighting scheme under different distributions of samples’ learning difficulty. It supports that the easy-first mode should be selected when there are excessive hard samples. The proposition for the occasion where there are excessive easy samples is shown in Section B.3.

**Concern 4: It is not clear to me how Proposition 1 helps the discussion.**

First of all, we need to understand that the sample distribution of the training and test sets may not be the same. The sample distribution of the test set is generally considered to be the same as that of the whole space. Therefore, the optimal model should perform best on the test set (whole space).

When there are excessive easy samples in a training set, the optimal model complexity on this training set will be lower than that of the whole sample space. Thus, we need to increase the optimal model complexity of this training set. 

Proposition 1 proves that increasing the weight of hard samples in a training set can increase the optimal model complexity of the current training data set. Thus, the increase of the optimal model complexity can be achieved by increasing the weight of hard samples, in other words, using the hard-first priority mode. 

Please let us know if there are any leftover concerns and we would be happy to do our utmost to address them.

content.title: A response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We want to thank all reviewers for the valuable comments. We have updated the latest version of our paper on arxiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.05481v3. 

In this version, we clearly show how theoretical analysis and experimental verification solve the four subproblems summarized in our paper.

Our proposed FlexW is only a solution (answer) when there is no prior knowledge or theoretical clues. FlexW can implement four priority modes, the optimal one can be selected based on the results of the hyper-parameter tuning. It is a scientific and effective method. Its performance is verified in our extensive experiments. If information about the difficulty distribution exists, the priority mode can be determined. The load of hyper-parameter tuning for FlexW will be decreased and the complexity of FlexW is similar to that of Focal loss.

We hope that the new version of our paper can eliminate your concerns.

Thank you again for your precious time.
